title: How to Plan a Feature Before You Touch the Code
content:
Before building “saved searches,” decide who saves them, what survives a refresh, and what happens when the underlying results change. A feature name can hide several different products. A short plan should expose those choices early enough that changing them costs a paragraph rather than a migration.

This guide proposes a compact planning artifact for a small product team. It combines a user problem, observable examples, boundaries, dependencies, and a release slice. It is an editorial method, not a requirement to produce a long specification before every reversible code edit.

Write the user's job and the current obstacle

Name a specific user and the task they are trying to complete. Describe what currently makes that task difficult. “Users need a dashboard” starts with a solution. “A support lead cannot see which unanswered requests are older than two days” identifies a job that several designs might serve.

The GOV.UK Service Manual's user-story guidance explains describing users, needs, and goals. Use that structure to sharpen the problem, then add the context your team needs. A sentence in a familiar format is helpful only if it distinguishes this user and task from a generic feature request.

Record who is outside the first version. A saved-search feature might initially support signed-in individuals but not shared team searches or notifications. Exclusions prevent a small implementation from silently inheriting requirements for collaboration, access control, and scheduled work.

Turn the idea into observable examples

Write a normal case, an invalid case, and a boundary case. For saved searches, the normal case might preserve a query and filters. An invalid case might reject an empty name. A boundary case might cover a filter that no longer exists when the search is reopened.

Cucumber's Gherkin reference describes structured scenarios using context, action, and outcome. You can borrow that clarity without adopting a new test framework. The important result is a concrete expectation that a designer, developer, and reviewer can interpret consistently.

Define success in terms of user behavior rather than internal implementation. “A saved search reopens with the same supported filters” is useful. “A database row exists” may be necessary evidence, but it does not show that the user can actually recover the search through the interface.

Map data and permission consequences

List the new information the feature stores, who owns it, and who can read or change it. Decide whether records belong to a user, workspace, or public collection. A frontend button hidden from other users does not establish server-side ownership checks. Put those expectations into the examples.

Consider deletion, updates, and compatibility. If the feature stores a reference to another object, what happens when that object disappears? If filters evolve, can old saved records still load? You do not need to predict every future version, but the first data model should make its assumptions explicit.

Identify external services and limits. A notification feature may require queues, email delivery, preference controls, and failure handling. If the first slice can solve the user problem without those dependencies, explain that choice. If they are essential, include them in the definition of complete rather than treating them as invisible follow-up work.

A hypothetical saved-search plan

Imagine a hypothetical directory adding saved searches for individual signed-in readers. The problem is repeated manual entry of the same filters. The first slice lets a reader name a search, reopen it, and delete it. Sharing and scheduled alerts are explicitly excluded.

The examples state that one reader cannot fetch another reader's saved record, an empty name produces a useful validation message, and an obsolete filter is reported rather than silently applied. The interface shows that results are current when reopened; it does not imply that the original result set was frozen.

The team chooses one end-to-end slice covering creation and reopening before adding bulk management. A local fixture exercises ownership and an obsolete filter. These are hypothetical planning choices, not claims that this feature was implemented or tested. The plan makes the first release's promise clear enough to evaluate.

Choose evidence and release boundaries

Say how the team will verify the examples. Some behavior belongs in a focused unit check, some at an API boundary, and some in a browser journey. Do not specify a large test suite merely to make the plan look thorough. Match evidence to the consequences and the boundary being protected.

List the deployment components and any migration. Decide how to disable the feature if an important assumption fails. A feature flag can hide an interface, but it may not stop background jobs or reverse data writes. Write the actual stopping behavior rather than using “rollback” as an unexplained reassurance.

Keep the plan short enough to review. Link existing research and technical detail instead of copying it all into one document. Mark unresolved decisions with an owner and the smallest next investigation. Planning is complete when implementation can proceed with known boundaries, not when every uncertainty has been eliminated.

Feature-planning checklist

  • Describe the user's task and current obstacle.
  • Name first-version exclusions.
  • Write observable examples, including permission failures.
  • Map ownership, data lifecycle, and compatibility.
  • Expose external dependencies and recovery needs.
  • Choose a small end-to-end slice.
  • Match verification to meaningful behavior.
  • Assign unresolved questions before coding begins.
excerpt: Plan a feature with a clear user problem, concrete behavior examples, data and permission boundaries, and a small end-to-end release slice.
